editorial_statement: Historical discoveries with modern educational research tasks; not breaking news, clinical advice, or claims of new experimental results

stories.title: The mold that changed medicine
stories.hook: Why weren't bacteria growing near the mold?
stories.intro: One unexpected observation grew into a powerful new way to treat infections—but only after many people did the hard work.

chapters.title: Something unusual appeared in a dish.
chapters.body: In 1928, Alexander Fleming noticed mold growing on a plate of bacteria. Around the mold, the bacteria were not growing normally.
chapters.takeaway: A surprise is only a clue. The first question is: can we observe it again?

chapters.title: Could the mold be releasing something?
chapters.body: Fleming investigated whether something made by the mold was stopping certain bacteria. He called the substance penicillin.
chapters.takeaway: Notice the difference between observing a result and explaining what caused it.

chapters.title: A finding in a dish was not yet a medicine.
chapters.body: Howard Florey, Ernst Chain, Norman Heatley and colleagues helped develop ways to isolate, test and produce penicillin. Moving from laboratory observations to patient treatment required years of additional work.
chapters.takeaway: Discovering a promising substance is different from proving it can be used safely and reliably.

chapters.title: Scientific progress often takes many hands.
chapters.body: Penicillin helped transform treatment for many bacterial infections. The original clue mattered, but later testing, production and medical evaluation mattered just as much.
chapters.takeaway: One verified observation can be valuable even when someone else performs the next experiment.

stories.tool_why: The original story is about a substance. PubChem helps researchers identify exactly which chemical they are talking about.
stories.tool_task: Open the Penicillin G page. Find the PubChem CID (compound ID). Write down the number and one alternate name.
stories.tool_answer: The page lists CID 5904 and the synonym benzylpenicillin.
stories.tool_limitation: Penicillin is a family of related antibiotics; this activity examines Penicillin G specifically. A chemical listing doesn't establish which medicine anyone should take.

stories.title: The teamwork that unlocked insulin
stories.hook: Could a missing body signal be replaced?
stories.intro: Scientists suspected the pancreas made something that controlled blood sugar. A team's experiments turned that idea into a treatment.

chapters.title: Why did losing the pancreas cause diabetes?
chapters.body: Researchers had linked the pancreas to blood sugar control, but the key internal substance was hard to isolate and use.
chapters.takeaway: A useful question often starts with an observation and something still missing.

chapters.title: Banting and Best tested a possibility.
chapters.body: In 1921, Frederick Banting and Charles Best, working with laboratory resources arranged by J. J. R. Macleod, tested pancreatic extracts in diabetic animals. The results were promising.
chapters.takeaway: Promising animal findings aren't proof that a treatment will work in people.

chapters.title: Cleaner extracts changed the outcome.
chapters.body: Biochemist James Collip improved purification. In January 1922, a more purified preparation produced a clear benefit for Leonard Thompson, an early patient. The first preparation had been less successful.
chapters.takeaway: Research often advances by improving and repeating an imperfect first attempt.

chapters.title: Breakthroughs need different skills.
chapters.body: Experimental design, laboratory work, chemical purification, clinical care and later large-scale production all contributed. The story is about collaboration, not a single magical moment.
chapters.takeaway: A contribution can be a better method, a verification, or a key improvement.

stories.tool_why: Insulin is made in a specific part of the body. The Human Protein Atlas lets you explore where the INS gene and insulin protein are found.
stories.tool_task: Open the INS pancreas page. Find which cells show high insulin protein expression, then note the location.
stories.tool_answer: The page reports high expression in pancreatic endocrine cells, with cytoplasmic staining in beta cells.
stories.tool_limitation: Tissue expression helps explain biology but does not establish a diagnosis, treatment dose, or outcome for an individual.
